Neural Wave Functions for High-Pressure Atomic Hydrogen

David Linteau Email: david.linteau@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Center for Quantum Science and Engineering, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Saverio Moroni Affiliation: CNR-IOM DEMOCRITOS, Istituto Officina dei Materiali and SISSA Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati, Via Bonomea 265, I-34136 Trieste, Italy    Giuseppe Carleo Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Center for Quantum Science and Engineering, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Markus Holzmann Affiliation: Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, LPMMC, 38000 Grenoble, France
Abstract

We leverage the power of neural quantum states to describe the ground state wave function of solid and liquid atomic hydrogen, including both electronic and protonic degrees of freedom. For static protons, the resulting Born-Oppenheimer energies are consistently comparable to or lower than all previous projector Monte Carlo results for systems containing up to 128128 hydrogen atoms. The same level of accuracy is preserved upon inclusion of nuclear quantum effects, thus going beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. In addition, our description overcomes major limitations of current wave functions, notably by avoiding any explicit symmetry assumption on the expected quantum crystal, and sidestepping efficiency issues of imaginary time evolution with disparate mass scales. As a first application, we examine crystal formation in an extremely high-density region up to pressure-induced melting.

Introduction–

Atomic and molecular hydrogen have played a fundamental role in the development of quantum mechanics and quantum chemistry. High-pressure experiments have revealed the existence of several unexpected molecular solid phases [1, 2] in the long-lasting search for atomic metallic hydrogen [3]. Despite the apparent simplicity, understanding the properties of high-pressure hydrogen and deuterium remains a formidable challenge for advanced first-principle simulation methods [4, 5].

Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) calculations [6] have provided some of the most accurate zero-temperature descriptions. However, hydrogen simulations remain challenging for two main reasons. First, the fixed-node approximation—inherent to DMC and required to circumvent the fermion sign problem—relies on trial wave functions of exceptional accuracy to capture the subtle physics of high-pressure phases. Second, inclusion of nuclear degrees of freedom substantially increases the computational cost: the Debye energy scale of atomic motion, much smaller than the Fermi energy scale of electrons, requires longer projection times in imaginary time evolution, and the very large proton-to-electron mass ratio (mp/me≃1836m_{p}/m_{e}\simeq 1836) implies much slower diffusion of the heavier particles [7]. These difficulties are shared by related methods like reptation Monte Carlo (RMC) and finite-temperature path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) [8, 9].

In this work, we show that Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) with neural quantum states (NQS) can overcome these limitations by using a flexible backflow wave function, enhanced by a graph neural network that couples electrons and protons. This approach naturally incorporates nuclear quantum effects beyond the Born–Oppenheimer approximation (BOA), a regime where conventional methods struggle due to mass-scale disparities.

Furthermore, our wave function avoids ad hoc symmetry constraints, a crucial feature for exploring high-pressure hydrogen phases where crystalline structures are unknown. As a first application, we study the onset of crystal formation in an ultra-dense region where pressure-induced melting is expected.

Since the first quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) studies on hydrogen [6, 7], only a few works have treated electronic and protonic degrees of freedom on equal footing [10, 11, 12]. Advances in QMC stem from decoupling electronic and protonic motions within the BOA. This underlies coupled electron ion Monte Carlo (CEIMC) [13] and ab-initio molecular dynamics (MD) [14] methods, operating at temperatures substantially below the electronic Fermi temperature, but high enough to describe nuclear motion within the adiabatic approximation (i.e. the BOA). Within the BOA, robust QMC trial wave functions are built from Hartree-Fock or density functional theory (DFT) band structure methods [15, 10, 11, 16], and improved with backflow coordinates [17]. The nuclear motion is then obtained via MD or PIMC [18, 4, 19], or, more recently, using deep network free energy methods [20, 21].

However, so far, CEIMC or MD simulations have been performed based on VMC calculations of the BOA energy surface. Although changes due to more accurate RMC or DMC values can be estimated a posteriori via reweighting of selected trajectories [22], or based on machine-learned force fields trained on DMC calculations of selected proton configurations [23, 24, 25, 26], the accuracy of the standard trial wave functions employed remains a major bottleneck of these methods. Therefore, we first benchmark our NQS on static proton configurations obtaining BOA energies that reach or surpass previous DMC/RMC values. This demonstrates the flexibility of backflow-based NQS for high-pressure hydrogen, as seen in studies of other systems such as atoms and molecules [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35], as well as electron matter [36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42].

We then address the ground state of the full Schrödinger equation of the combined electron-proton system—the “dynamic” case—thereby going beyond the BOA. Unlike BOA wave functions with orbitals tied to a fixed proton configuration, our NQS explicitly incorporates proton motion via a factor capturing zero-point motion. Whereas projection methods, such as DMC and RMC, are burdened by mass-dependent convergence issues (as the kinetic energy of the propagator ties the diffusion of the particles to their inverse mass), in VMC the convergence does not depend on the nuclear mass, because Monte Carlo updates can be addressed on the appropriate scale for each type of particle. Finally, our ansatz accurately describes liquid and solid phases in a translationally invariant form, without imposing a particular crystal symmetry [43, 44], which is crucial for high-pressure hydrogen where the phase diagram is not fully determined. We present preliminary results in the region where atomic hydrogen is expected to melt at ultra-high pressures.

Method–

We consider NN hydrogen atoms in a simulation cell of volume V=4​π​N​rs3​a03/3V=4\pi Nr_{s}^{3}a_{0}^{3}/3, where rs=a/a0r_{s}=a/a_{0} parametrizes the electronic number density, with aa and a0a_{0} being the mean electronic distance and the Bohr radius, respectively. To simplify the notation, we will focus on the case of a cubic box of extension L=V1/3L=V^{1/3} in the following. We denote the electron and proton coordinates by {𝐫i}\{\mathbf{r}_{i}\} and {𝐑I}\{\mathbf{R}_{I}\}, respectively. As we simultaneously sample both sets of coordinates using Monte Carlo, a configuration is denoted 𝐗≡{𝐫,𝐑}≡{𝐫1,…,𝐫N,𝐑1,…,𝐑N}\mathbf{X}\equiv\{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R}\}\equiv\{\mathbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{N},\mathbf{R}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{N}\}. We periodize the simulation cell so that the Hamiltonian in atomic units reads

H=−∑a=12​N12​ma∇𝐱a2+12∑𝐧∈ℤ𝟑∑a,b=12​N′qa​qb|𝐱a−𝐱b+𝐧​L|,H=-\sum_{a=1}^{2N}\frac{1}{2m_{a}}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{a}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}}\sum_{a,b=1}^{2N}{}^{\hskip-2.84526pt{}^{\prime}}\frac{q_{a}q_{b}}{|\mathbf{x}_{a}-\mathbf{x}_{b}+\mathbf{n}L|}, (1)

where 𝐱a∈𝐗\mathbf{x}_{a}\in\mathbf{X}, mam_{a} and qaq_{a} are respectively the mass and electric charge of particle aa. The restriction on the Coulomb sum, denoted by an apostrophe, specifies that 𝐧=𝟎\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{0} is omitted when a=ba=b. The Ewald procedure [45] is used to evaluate the (conditionally convergent) second term in Eq. 1.

To construct a ground state trial wave function, it is convenient to consider the following general form

Ψ⁡(𝐗)=Φ⁡(𝐑)​det​[ϕk​(𝐫i|𝐗)]​e−U⁡(𝐗),\Psi(\mathbf{X})=\Phi(\mathbf{R})\mathrm{det}[\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r}_{i}|\mathbf{X})]e^{-U(\mathbf{X})}, (2)

where U⁡(𝐗)U(\mathbf{X}) denotes a symmetric correlation factor, Φ⁡(𝐑)\Phi(\mathbf{R}) is a pure nuclear wave function, and {ϕk​(𝐫i|𝐗)}\{\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r}_{i}|\mathbf{X})\} is a set of electronic orbitals, with 1≤k≤N1\leq k\leq N, which may symmetrically depend on all coordinates in 𝐗\mathbf{X} that are different from 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}. Although this form is general for all fermionic ground state wave functions [46, 47, 48], there is no guarantee that the orbitals ϕk​(𝐫i|𝐗)\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r}_{i}|\mathbf{X}) can be efficiently represented numerically.

In the first calculations on dense hydrogen [6, 7], U⁡(𝐗)U(\mathbf{X}) was chosen as a sum of pairwise correlation factors in terms of electron-electron (e-e), electron-proton (e-p) and proton-proton (p-p) pseudo-potentials. The orbital part of the wave function consisted of Slater determinants for spin-up and spin-down electrons occupying either plane wave orbitals with wave vectors 𝐤\mathbf{k} inside the Fermi surface, or Gaussians localized at the crystalline lattice sites, denoted {𝐑I(0)}\{\mathbf{R}_{I}^{(0)}\}. Later calculations [11] have used orbitals from DFT within the local-density approximation (LDA), with the orbitals also pinned at {𝐑I(0)}\{\mathbf{R}_{I}^{(0)}\}. Exchange effects for protons (and deuterium) are expected to be small in the crystalline phase [6]. Quantum statistical effects on protons have thus been neglected, and the proton crystal was described by the asymmetric (Nosanow) wave function Φ⁡(𝐑)=∏Iφ⁡(|𝐑I−𝐑I(0)|)\Phi(\mathbf{R})=\prod_{I}\varphi(|\mathbf{R}_{I}-\mathbf{R}_{I}^{(0)}|) [49, 50], where φ\varphi is a Gaussian function with a width variational parameter to optimize. Although DMC stochastically improves the wave function via imaginary time projection, in practice the results are strongly biased by the explicit dependence on the assumed crystalline structure. Full exploration of the nuclear phase space in imaginary time is difficult due to the large mass imbalance between protons and electrons. We note that the effect is amplified when considering deuterium having twice the proton’s mass, obeying bosonic nuclear statistics. Backflow and three-body correlations in hydrogen [17] have shown to improve energies also for the fully dynamic protons at zero-temperature [12], but have not been explored further since.

Our wave function builds upon these previous ones by incorporating two important modifications. First, as electronic orbitals we use

ϕ𝐤σ​(𝐫i)=∑𝐧∈ℤ3∑I=1Nei​𝐤⋅(𝐑I+𝐧​L)​χ​(𝐫iσ−𝐑I−𝐧​L),\phi_{\mathbf{k}}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\sum_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\sum_{I=1}^{N}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{R}_{I}+\mathbf{n}L)}\chi(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\sigma}-\mathbf{R}_{I}-\mathbf{n}L), (3)

which coincide with Bloch functions for static protons on a crystalline lattice. For χ\chi, we have chosen a Gaussian with a free width parameter. While these radially symmetric s-orbitals seem to be sufficient at describing the range of densities studied in this work, angular dependence via higher orbitals (p, d, f, etc.) can be included in a straightforward manner.

Second, we increase the expressivity of the trial wave function by adding propagator-like backflow to the electron coordinates,

𝐫i→𝐫i+W​𝐲i(b),\mathbf{r}_{i}\to\mathbf{r}_{i}+W\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(b)}, (4)

where 𝐲i(b)\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(b)} is the electron vertex output of a message-passing neural network (MPNN) after bb iterations, and WW is a matrix of complex variational parameters. This electron backflow is only added in the orbital part of the wave function. For U⁡(𝐗)U(\mathbf{X}), we take advantage of the electron edge output of the MPNN, denoted by 𝐘i​j(b)\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(b)}, to create a propagator-like term, similarly as in Ref. [44]. With this additional piece the correlation factor U⁡(𝐗)U(\mathbf{X}) reads

U⁡(𝐱)→U⁡(𝐱)+∑i<j[w​MLP​(𝐘i​j(b))],U(\mathbf{x})\to U(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{i<j}\left[w\ \mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(b)})\right], (5)

where MLP stands for multilayer perceptron and w∈ℝw\in\mathbb{R} is a variational parameter. The MPNN operates on two underlying graphs: the electron one and the proton one, which interact at each message-passing iteration. In particular, it involves e-e and e-p contributions, meaning that the resulting backflow involve both the electron and proton coordinates, with the e-p contributions capturing a smaller—though important—part of the correlation (see Appendix A).

This corresponds to a modified version of the message-passing neural quantum state architecture introduced in Ref. [51]. In the dynamic case, when the protons are not localized to lattice sites, the zero-point motion of the protons is captured with the edge output 𝐘I​J(b)\mathbf{Y}_{IJ}^{(b)} of a different MPNN than the electronic one, which is processed similarly as in Eq. 5. This latter MPNN operates only on a single graph—the proton one.

Although we can reach large system sizes of around 10210^{2} particles with our implementation (see the Results section), important finite-size effects remain, which can be addressed from strategies discussed in Ref. [52]. Most important, especially for metallic systems, are shell effects due to the sharp Fermi surface. These shell effects can however be strongly reduced by employing twist-averaged boundary conditions (TABC) [53], which, for a displacement of particle ii by one lattice vector L​𝐞αL\mathbf{e}_{\alpha} along direction α\alpha, impose the following constraint on the wave function

Ψ⁡({𝐫j+δi​j​L​𝐞α},𝐑)=ei​ϑα​Ψ​({𝐫j},𝐑),\Psi(\{\mathbf{r}_{j}+\delta_{ij}L\mathbf{e}_{\alpha}\},\mathbf{R})=e^{i\vartheta_{\alpha}}\Psi(\{\mathbf{r}_{j}\},\mathbf{R}), (6)

where 𝐞α\mathbf{e}_{\alpha} denotes the unit vector in the direction of α∈{x,y,z}\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}, with −π≤ϑα<π-\pi\leq\vartheta_{\alpha}<\pi, and i,ji,j labels any of the electron coordinates. We remark that we have only imposed TABC on the electronic degrees of freedom. Periodic boundary conditions (PBC) correspond to the special case where the twist angle is trivial, that is ϑ≡(ϑx,ϑy,ϑz)=𝟎\bm{\vartheta}\equiv(\vartheta_{x},\vartheta_{y},\vartheta_{z})=\bm{0}. We can impose TABC on the wave function by selecting the “twisted” wave vector 𝐤=(2​π​𝐦+ϑ)/L\mathbf{k}=(2\pi\mathbf{m}+\bm{\vartheta})/L, with 𝐦∈ℤ3\mathbf{m}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}, for the electronic orbitals. In practice, the electron orbitals are then filled by taking the twisted wave vectors with the smallest norm.

Results–

As a first step, we want to establish the accuracy of our NQS compared to previous VMC and DMC results. Prior calculations have almost exclusively focused on BOA ground state of electrons using the external (Coulomb) potential of the static protons. Formally, the electronic Hamiltonian, He​(𝐑)H_{e}(\mathbf{R}), corresponds to infinite proton mass in Eq. (1),

He(𝐑)=−12​me∑i=1N∇𝐫i2+12∑𝐧∈ℤ𝟑∑a,b=12​Nqa​qb|𝐱a−𝐱b+𝐧​L|′.H_{e}(\mathbf{R})=-\frac{1}{2m_{e}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_{i}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}}\sum_{a,b=1}^{2N}{}^{\hskip-2.84526pt{}^{\prime}}\frac{q_{a}q_{b}}{|\mathbf{x}_{a}-\mathbf{x}_{b}+\mathbf{n}L|}. (7)

To obtain upper bounds to the BOA ground state energies, we minimize He​(𝐑)H_{e}(\mathbf{R}) over electronic wave functions Ψe​(𝐫|𝐑)\Psi_{e}(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{R}) with purely parametric dependence on 𝐑\mathbf{R}. We have used the same functional form as in Eq. 2, simply treating the protonic coordinates as (external) static parameters. Additional implicit parametric dependence on 𝐑\mathbf{R} may be introduced via the optimization parameters.

In Table 1, we compare our results for static protons localized on a perfect body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice around metallization, at rs=1.31r_{s}=1.31, with DMC calculations using Slater-Jastrow (SJ) and backflow wave functions with metallic plane wave orbitals [17], as well as with LDA-DFT orbitals [11] and backflow augmented PBE-DFT orbitals (BF-PBE) [54]. Calculations have been performed for N=16N=16, 5454, and 128128 electrons under PBC. Our VMC results systematically lower the energies per atom by ∼1\sim 1 mHa compared to the best SJ-DMC calculations reported in the literature, and perform similarly to RMC results with BF-PBE wave functions. The quality of the wave function is further quantified by roughly a fivefold reduction in variance compared to the SJ-VMC wave function underlying the DMC calculation. Notably, about the same improvement is obtained for all three system sizes using a total of 2889 parameters, illustrating the size consistency of our wave function and of the results.

In Table 3 (see Appendix B), we further provide explicit comparisons of twist-averaged calculations for static protons in different crystal structures obtained with RMC in Ref. [16], which also provide DFT orbitals augmented with backflow wave functions, as used in CEIMC calculations. Again, our NQS is able to compete with the best projector Monte Carlo results, in this case RMC based on LDA or optimized independent particle (IPP) orbitals augmented with backflow.

So far, we have shown that our NQS wave function reaches and improves on previous DMC energies from the literature by focusing on high-symmetry configurations of atomic hydrogen. Our NQS state can therefore serve to enhance the accuracy of machine-learned effective potentials for hydrogen atoms [55, 56, 57, 23, 24, 25, 58, 59, 26], to benchmark DFT functionals on representative proton configurations in the atomic regime of the high-pressure phase diagram [60, 61], and to further achieve DMC/RMC-level precision of the BOA energy surface in future CEIMC or MD calculations.

We have further explored the expressivity of our ansatz in the molecular phases at lower pressures. Comparing to generic configurations with N=96N=96 protons provided in the dense hydrogen DMC database from Ref. [24, 62], spanning molecular solid and liquid configurations at pressures from 50 to 200 GPa, our present NQS architecture remains roughly 2-5 mHa above the DMC reference energies, indicating limitations of our orbitals in the molecular phases. Further work is needed to reduce the systematic bias of our ansatz in the molecular region to simultaneously capture both molecular and atomic phases using a universal ansatz, similar to recent foundation models [63, 32, 31]. Details on the global optimization scheme that can be used for such universal ansätze, as well as preliminary results, are provided in Appendix C.

We finally present the calculations of ground state energies with dynamical protons without relying on the BOA. There, electronic and protonic degrees of freedom are sampled according to the full wave function, given in Eq. 2, and energies are obtained from minimizing the expectation value of HH, given in Eq. 1. Effects beyond BOA are naturally included in the evaluation of the protons’ kinetic energy, acting on the purely nuclear part Φ⁡(𝐑)\Phi(\mathbf{R}), as well as on the electronic wave function Ψe​(𝐫|𝐑)\Psi_{e}(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{R}). As a first benchmark, we consider hydrogen at rs=1.31r_{s}=1.31, with localized Gaussians for the nuclear wave function Φ⁡(𝐑)\Phi(\mathbf{R}), so that the proton positions fluctuate around BCC lattice sites. This allows us to faithfully compare in Table 2 with VMC and DMC results from Ref. [12], based on BF-PW and SJ-LDA trial wave functions. Again, improvement is consistently obtained. To provide more insights into the structure of the optimized wave function, we further show in Fig. 1 pair correlation functions between different particle types (electrons, protons and spin-up electrons), as well as Monte Carlo configurations in position space showcasing the BCC lattice structure.

We finally fully relax the nuclear wave function—keeping the wave function fully translationally invariant—and explore the ground state structures of N=8N=8 atoms under increasing compression. The associated nuclear wave function Φ⁡(𝐑)\Phi(\mathbf{R}) is constructed with 𝐘I​J(b)\mathbf{Y}_{IJ}^{(b)}, as described above, as well as a p-p pseudo-potential. Importantly, it does not involve a product of Gaussian functions localizing the protons at lattice sites. Fig. 2 shows the (proton-proton) pair correlation function in three dimensional space, at various pressures near the expected melting transition. The method used is clearly able to find structural changes when increasing the pressure (or lowering rsr_{s}) and the system turns liquid around rs≈0.2r_{s}\approx 0.2. However, studies at larger system sizes and different cell geometries are required to precisely determine the crystalline structures as well as the exact melting density. So far, pressure-induced melting of hydrogen has only been studied from approximate matching of hydrogen to calculations for the one-component plasma [64], or based on an approximate Thomas-Fermi screening model that uses a Yukawa pair-potential for the proton-proton interaction [65, 66, 67].

The NQS-based approach presented here enables the direct identification and characterization of atomic crystalline hydrogen structures and their melting transition, and is only limited in this study by finite-size effects.

Although melting occurs at ultra-high densities, the inter-protonic distance apa^{p} remains larger than the protonic Bohr radius (a0p≡a0​me/mpa_{0}^{p}\equiv a_{0}m_{e}/m_{p}), that is, ap/a0p≃1836​rs≫1a^{p}/a_{0}^{p}\simeq 1836\,r_{s}\gg 1. This justifies neglecting fermionic statistics in the solid phase, which means in practice that no protonic determinants are included in the wave function. Finite-size effects, by imposing TABC for instance, as well as Fermi statistics for protons and isotope effects, will be addressed in future work.

Conclusion–

We have introduced a neural quantum state that accurately describes electron-ion systems. Validated against RMC and DMC results, our method achieves high precision for high-pressure atomic hydrogen both in the Born–Oppenheimer regime and for the full zero–temperature ground state beyond BOA. Our preliminary study demonstrates that our NQS can capture the zero–temperature melting of atomic hydrogen while treating protons and electrons on equal footing. These attributes pave the way for an extensive exploration of the high–pressure phase diagram for both hydrogen and deuterium. Moreover, the incorporation of nuclear quantum statistics opens promising avenues for studying isotope effects and nuclear spin phenomena such as the ortho–para transitions in molecular hydrogen.

The simulations were performed using NetKet [68, 69], built on JAX [70] and mpi4jax [71]. The data underlying the figures, together with the code used to generate them, are publicly available in the GitHub repository [72]. The Laplacian was evaluated using the forward Laplacian method [73], implemented via either folx [74] or fwdlap [75].

The data that supports the findings of this article are openly available [72].

Appendix A Message-passing neural network (MPNN) implementation

The implementation used in this work is detailed in Algorithm 1. Other recent MPNN implementations for NQS were presented for instance in [51, 76, 77, 44].

 

Algorithm 1 MPNN

 

Data– Given a Monte-Carlo configuration ((𝐫1,s1),…,(𝐫N,sN),𝐑1,…,𝐑N)((\mathbf{r}_{1},s_{1}),\ldots,(\mathbf{r}_{N},s_{N}),\mathbf{R}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{N}), where sis_{i} is an electron spin label, the following electron-electron and electron-proton input tensors can be constructed:

𝐈i​j\displaystyle\mathbf{I}_{ij} =[sin⁡(2​π​𝐫i​j/L),cos⁡(2​π​𝐫i​j/L),|sin⁡(π​𝐫i​j/L)|,si​sj]∈ℝ2​d+2,\displaystyle=[\sin(2\pi\mathbf{r}_{ij}/L),\cos(2\pi\mathbf{r}_{ij}/L),|\sin(\pi\mathbf{r}_{ij}/L)|,s_{i}s_{j}]\in\mathbb{R}^{2d+2}, (8)
𝐈i​I\displaystyle\mathbf{I}_{iI} =[sin⁡(2​π​𝐫i​I/L),cos⁡(2​π​𝐫i​I/L),|sin⁡(π​𝐫i​I/L)|]∈ℝ2​d+1,\displaystyle=[\sin(2\pi\mathbf{r}_{iI}/L),\cos(2\pi\mathbf{r}_{iI}/L),|\sin(\pi\mathbf{r}_{iI}/L)|]\in\mathbb{R}^{2d+1}, (9)

where 𝐫i​j=𝐫i−𝐫j\mathbf{r}_{ij}=\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}, 𝐫i​I=𝐫i−𝐑I\mathbf{r}_{iI}=\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I} and the square brackets correspond to the concatenation operation. The following hyperparameters have to be fixed by the user: the hidden dimension hh, the attention dimension aa, the MLP output dimension ee, and the number of message-passing iteration(s) bb.

(The vector or matrix dimension is shown below as a comment on the right.)
Initialization– instantiate “hidden” embedding parameters 𝐡i(0),𝐇i​j(0),𝐇i​I(0)\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(0)},\mathbf{H}_{ij}^{(0)},\mathbf{H}_{iI}^{(0)} ⊳h\triangleright\ h
Define vertex states 𝐲i(0)=𝐡i(0)\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(0)}=\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(0)} ⊳h\triangleright\ h
Define edge states 𝐘i​j(0)=[𝐈i​j,𝐇i​j(0)]\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(0)}=[\mathbf{I}_{ij},\mathbf{H}_{ij}^{(0)}], 𝐘i​I(0)=[𝐈i​I,𝐇i​I(0)]\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(0)}=[\mathbf{I}_{iI},\mathbf{H}_{iI}^{(0)}] ⊳ 2​d+2+h, 2​d+1+h\triangleright\ 2d+2+h,\ 2d+1+h
for 0≤ℓ≤b0\leq\ell\leq b do
Electron-proton edge update:
Initialize query and key matrices Qe​p(ℓ),Ke​p(ℓ)Q_{ep}^{(\ell)},\ K_{ep}^{(\ell)} ⊳dim(𝐘i​I(ℓ))×a\triangleright\ \mathrm{dim}(\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell)})\times a
Compute queries and keys 𝐐i​I(ℓ)=Qe​p(ℓ)​𝐘i​I(ℓ),𝐊i​I(ℓ)=Ke​p(ℓ)​𝐘i​I(ℓ)\mathbf{Q}_{iI}^{(\ell)}=Q_{ep}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell)},\ \ \mathbf{K}_{iI}^{(\ell)}=K_{ep}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell)} ⊳a\triangleright\ a
Compute attention weights 𝐖i​I(ℓ)=MLPe​p,1(ℓ)​(𝐐(ℓ)​𝐊(ℓ)/a)i​I\mathbf{W}_{iI}^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{MLP}_{ep,1}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{Q}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}/\sqrt{a})_{iI} ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Compute messages 𝐌i​I(ℓ)=𝐖i​I(ℓ)⊙MLPe​p,2(ℓ)​(𝐘i​I(ℓ))\mathbf{M}_{iI}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{W}_{iI}^{(\ell)}\odot\mathrm{MLP}_{ep,2}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell)}) ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Update edge hidden states 𝐇i​I(ℓ+1)=MLPe​p,3(ℓ)​([𝐘i​I(ℓ),𝐌i​I(ℓ)])\mathbf{H}_{iI}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathrm{MLP}_{ep,3}^{(\ell)}([\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{M}_{iI}^{(\ell)}]) ⊳e\triangleright\ e

Update edge states 𝐘i​I(ℓ+1)=[𝐈i​I,𝐇i​I(ℓ+1)]\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell+1)}=[\mathbf{I}_{iI},\mathbf{H}_{iI}^{(\ell+1)}] ⊳ 2​d+1+e\triangleright\ 2d+1+e
Electron-electron edge and vertex update:
Initialize query and key matrices Qe​e(ℓ),Ke​e(ℓ)Q_{ee}^{(\ell)},\ K_{ee}^{(\ell)} ⊳dim(𝐘i​j(ℓ))×a\triangleright\ \mathrm{dim}(\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(\ell)})\times a
Compute queries and keys 𝐐i​j(ℓ)=Qe​e(ℓ)​𝐘i​j(ℓ),𝐊i​j(ℓ)=Ke​e(ℓ)​𝐘i​j(ℓ)\mathbf{Q}_{ij}^{(\ell)}=Q_{ee}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(\ell)},\ \ \mathbf{K}_{ij}^{(\ell)}=K_{ee}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(\ell)} ⊳a\triangleright\ a
Compute attention weights 𝐖i​j(ℓ)=MLPe​e,1(ℓ)​(𝐐(ℓ)​𝐊(ℓ)/a)i​j\mathbf{W}_{ij}^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{MLP}_{ee,1}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{Q}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}/\sqrt{a})_{ij} ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Compute messages 𝐌i​j(ℓ)=𝐖i​j(ℓ)⊙MLPe​e,2(ℓ)​(𝐘i​j(ℓ))\mathbf{M}_{ij}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{W}_{ij}^{(\ell)}\odot\mathrm{MLP}_{ee,2}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(\ell)}) ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Compute vertex cross-species contributions: 𝐂i(ℓ)=∑IMLPe​e,3​(𝐘i​I(ℓ+1))\mathbf{C}_{i}^{(\ell)}=\sum_{I}\mathrm{MLP}_{ee,3}(\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell+1)}) ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Compute edge cross-species contributions: 𝐂i​j(ℓ)=∑IMLPe​e,4​(𝐘i​I(ℓ+1))⊙MLPe​e,5​(𝐘j​I(ℓ+1))\mathbf{C}_{ij}^{(\ell)}=\sum_{I}\mathrm{MLP}_{ee,4}(\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(\ell+1)})\odot\mathrm{MLP}_{ee,5}(\mathbf{Y}_{jI}^{(\ell+1)}) ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Update vertex hidden states 𝐡i(ℓ+1)=MLPe​e,6(ℓ)​([𝐡i(ℓ),∑j𝐌i​j(ℓ),𝐂i(ℓ)])\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathrm{MLP}_{ee,6}^{(\ell)}([\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(\ell)},\sum_{j}\mathbf{M}_{ij}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{C}_{i}^{(\ell)}]) ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Update edge hidden states 𝐇i​j(ℓ+1)=MLPe​e,7(ℓ)​([𝐘i​j(ℓ),𝐌i​j(ℓ),𝐂i​j(ℓ)])\mathbf{H}_{ij}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathrm{MLP}_{ee,7}^{(\ell)}([\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{M}_{ij}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{C}_{ij}^{(\ell)}]) ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Update vertex states 𝐲i(ℓ+1)=𝐡i(ℓ+1)\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(\ell+1)}=\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(\ell+1)} ⊳e\triangleright\ e
Update edge states 𝐘i​j(ℓ+1)=[𝐈i​j,𝐇i​j(ℓ+1)]\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(\ell+1)}=[\mathbf{I}_{ij},\mathbf{H}_{ij}^{(\ell+1)}] ⊳ 2​d+2+e\triangleright\ 2d+2+e
end for
return final vertex and edge states 𝐲i(b),𝐘i​j(b),𝐘i​I(b)\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(b)},\mathbf{Y}_{ij}^{(b)},\mathbf{Y}_{iI}^{(b)}

 

Appendix B Energy comparison for various crystal structures

In Table 3, we compare twist-averaged (TABC) calculations for static protons with different crystal structures, as well as different NN and rsr_{s}, with the best reptation Monte Carlo (RMC) results from Ref. [78, 16], obtained either by using backflow augmented metallic (BF-PW), DFT (BF-LDA), or optimized independent particle potential (BF-IPP) orbitals. All TABC results are based on a 6×6×66\times 6\times 6 twist grid. The NQS results were obtained with a 6×6×66\times 6\times 6 Monkhorst-Pack grid [79], providing twist grid convergence within ∼0.5\sim 0.5 mHa. We further provide PBC energies to facilitate the comparison for future work. We find that the NQS generally performs as good or better than the RMC wave functions, except for the diamond lattice where NQS energies are slightly higher.

Appendix C Global optimization of a universal wave function

In developing a foundation model for electronic structure, the objective is to optimize a single set of variational parameters, 𝜽\bm{\theta}, so that the electronic ground state wave function Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R}) accurately describes a set of electronic Hamiltonians {He​(𝐑)}𝐑\{H_{e}(\mathbf{R})\}_{\mathbf{R}} (with He​(𝐑)H_{e}(\mathbf{R}) defined in Eq. 7) associated with different static nuclear configurations {𝐑}\{\mathbf{R}\}, with 𝐑={𝐑1,…,𝐑N}\mathbf{R}=\{\mathbf{R}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{N}\}. In the most general form, the associated global variational energy Eglobal​(𝜽)E_{\mathrm{global}}(\bm{\theta}) is given by

Eglobal​(𝜽)=∫d​𝐑​𝒫​(𝐑)​⟨Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)|He​(𝐑(i))|Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)⟩⟨Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)|Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)⟩,E_{\mathrm{global}}(\bm{\theta})=\int d\mathbf{R}\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R})\frac{\langle\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R})|H_{e}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R})\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R})|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R})\rangle}, (10)

where the expectation value ⟨…⟩\langle\dots\hskip-0.02864pt\rangle is taken over a sufficiently large set of electronic configurations {𝐫}\{\mathbf{r}\}, with 𝐫={𝐫1,…,𝐫N}\mathbf{r}=\{\mathbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{N}\} (assuming the same number of electrons as nuclei without loss of generality), from the conditional probability density P𝜽​(𝐫|𝐑)=|⟨Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)|𝐫⟩|2/⟨Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)|Ψ𝜽​(𝐑)⟩P_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{r}|\mathbf{R})=|\langle\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R})|\mathbf{r}\rangle|^{2}/\langle\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R})|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R})\rangle. In practice, the integration over the reference probability distribution 𝒫⁡(𝐑)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}) is performed through Monte Carlo averages obtained using a finite set of MM independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) nuclear configurations drawn from 𝒫⁡(𝐑)\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}), that is, 𝐑∼𝒫⁡(𝐑)\mathbf{R}\sim\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}). Assuming the nuclear configurations are re-sampled uniformly from an existing dataset of configurations, 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the integral reduces to the following discrete form

Eglobal​(𝜽)=1M​∑i=1M⟨Ψ𝜽​(𝐑(i))|He​(𝐑(i))|Ψ𝜽​(𝐑(i))⟩⟨Ψ𝜽​(𝐑(i))|Ψ𝜽​(𝐑(i))⟩≡1M​∑i=1ME⁡(𝐑(i),𝜽),E_{\mathrm{global}}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\frac{\langle\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})|H_{e}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})\rangle}\equiv\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}E(\mathbf{R}^{(i)},\bm{\theta}), (11)

where a uniform distribution 𝒫⁡(𝐑)=1/M\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R})=1/M is implicitly used and each nuclear configuration 𝐑(i)\mathbf{R}^{(i)} is part of the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, i.e. 𝐑(i)∈𝒟\mathbf{R}^{(i)}\in\mathcal{D}. We further implicitly defined the expectation value of He​(𝐑(i))H_{e}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)}) with respect to the globally optimized wave function Ψ𝜽\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}, evaluated at the set of (global) variational parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} and at one nuclear configuration 𝐑(i)\mathbf{R}^{(i)}, as E⁡(𝐑(i),𝜽)E(\mathbf{R}^{(i)},\bm{\theta}). The global optimization strategy we propose, analogous to the framework described in the Foundation Neural-Network Quantum States paper [63], leverages an extended stochastic reconfiguration (SR) scheme [80, 81, 82] for multiple auxiliary systems (here each labeled by the nuclear configuration 𝐑\mathbf{R}). For completeness, we rewrite this procedure, simply adapting the notation, which states that the variational parameter update 𝜹​𝜽\bm{\delta\theta} is given by the following matrix equation

𝒮​𝜹​𝜽=−η​𝐅,\mathcal{S}\bm{\delta\theta}=-\eta\mathbf{F}, (12)

where the quantum geometric tensor 𝒮\mathcal{S} has size P×PP\times P, with PP the total number of variational parameters, η\eta is the learning rate and 𝐅=∇𝜽Eglobal​(𝜽)\mathbf{F}=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}E_{\mathrm{global}}(\bm{\theta}) is the gradient of the loss function. The component of the latter ℱk∈𝐅\mathcal{F}_{k}\in\mathbf{F}, with k∈1,…,Pk\in{1,\ldots,P}, are formally defined as ℱk=∫d​𝐑​𝒫​(𝐑)​Fk​(𝐑)\mathcal{F}_{k}=\int d\mathbf{R}\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R})F_{k}(\mathbf{R}), where Fk​(𝐑)F_{k}(\mathbf{R}) can be written as a covariance of the form

Fk​(𝐑)\displaystyle F_{k}(\mathbf{R}) =−2​R​e​{⟨Δ​Ok†​(𝐑)​Δ​He​(𝐑)⟩}\displaystyle=-2\mathrm{Re}\{\langle\Delta O_{k}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{R})\Delta H_{e}(\mathbf{R})\rangle\}
=−2​R​e​{⟨Ok†​(𝐑)​He​(𝐑)⟩−⟨He​(𝐑)⟩​⟨Ok†​(𝐑)⟩},\displaystyle=-2\mathrm{Re}\{\langle O_{k}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{R})H_{e}(\mathbf{R})\rangle-\langle H_{e}(\mathbf{R})\rangle\langle O_{k}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{R})\rangle\}, (13)

where Δ​A=A−⟨A⟩\Delta A=A-\langle A\rangle corresponds to the shifted-mean operator of an arbitrary operator AA, and Ok​(𝐑)=∂ln⁡Ψ𝜽​(𝐫,𝐑)/∂θkO_{k}(\mathbf{R})=\partial\ln\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{R})/\partial\theta_{k}, with θk∈𝜽\theta_{k}\in\bm{\theta}. The extension of the quantum geometric tensor to the extended space is performed similarly, so that 𝒮k​l=∫d​𝐑​𝒫​(𝐑)​Sk​l​(𝐑)\mathcal{S}_{kl}=\int d\mathbf{R}\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R})S_{kl}(\mathbf{R}), with

Sk​l​(𝐑)\displaystyle S_{kl}(\mathbf{R}) =Re⁡{⟨Δ​Ok†​(𝐑)​Δ​Ol​(𝐑)⟩}\displaystyle=\mathrm{Re}\{\langle\Delta O_{k}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{R})\Delta O_{l}(\mathbf{R})\rangle\}
=Re⁡{⟨Ok†​(𝐑)​Ol​(𝐑)⟩−⟨Ok†​(𝐑)⟩​⟨Ol​(𝐑)⟩}.\displaystyle=\mathrm{Re}\{\langle O^{\dagger}_{k}(\mathbf{R})O_{l}(\mathbf{R})\rangle-\langle O_{k}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{R})\rangle\langle O_{l}(\mathbf{R})\rangle\}. (14)

This global optimization scheme contrasts sharply with the conventional approach of individually optimizing the electronic wave function for each nuclear configuration. Although the latter will generally provide more accurate absolute energies, it is exceedingly inefficient for large datasets and requires extensive computational resources and human intervention.

In the context of high-pressure hydrogen, we considered the Dense hydrogen DMC database [24, 62], that we denote as 𝒟\mathcal{D}, containing |𝒟|=17 528|\mathcal{D}|=17\,528 configurations spanning pressures from 50 to 200 GPa and temperatures from 600 to 2200 K. For preliminary testing, we restrict our attention to the 50 GPa subset 𝒟50={x∈𝒟:P⁡(x)=50​GPa}\mathcal{D}_{50}=\{x\in\mathcal{D}:P(x)=50\ \mathrm{GPa}\} with |𝒟50|=2 469|\mathcal{D}_{50}|=2\,469. A training set 𝒞⊂𝒟50\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{D}_{50} of size M=512M=512 is selected without imposing any temperature bias, leaving |𝒟50∖𝒞|=1 957|\mathcal{D}_{50}\setminus\mathcal{C}|=1\,957 configurations outside the learning set. The pressure of P=50P=50 GPa was chosen as it lies farthest from the metallic regime, allowing us to test the wave function beyond the metallic phase where it performs well. We then obtained an optimized set of parameters 𝜽∗\bm{\theta}^{*} by minimizing Eq. 11 over this subset of configurations 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In particular, the SR scheme described above was used to optimize all the 2889 parameters included in the trial wave function.

Using a 4×4×44\times 4\times 4 twist grid (matching the protocol of Refs. [24, 62]), the average difference between the global NQS and DMC reference energies (per electron), given by

Δ​E=1M​∑i=1M(E⁡(𝐑(i),𝜽∗)N−Eref​(𝐑(i))N),\Delta E=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left(\frac{E(\mathbf{R}^{(i)},\bm{\theta}^{*})}{N}-\frac{E_{\mathrm{ref}}(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})}{N}\right), (15)

is Δ​E∼4\Delta E\sim 4 mHa for configurations included in the training set, and Δ​E∼5\Delta E\sim 5 mHa for configurations excluded from the training set but still tagged with a DFT pressure of P=50P=50 GPa (defining a so-called test set). (Note that we have not corrected for two-body finite size effects [52] in both NQS and database DMC energies.) As hinted in the main text, the global optimization results’ accuracy is therefore not yet satisfactory, being on average more than 4 mHa away from the reference energies, leaving a lot of place for improvement.

However, in terms of the computation time, the global optimization routine ran once on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU for approximately 72 hours, with an additional 15 hours required to compute 500 test-set energies, for instance, amounting to roughly 100 GPU hours in total. In contrast, a conventional DMC procedure, in which the electronic wave function is independently optimized for each configuration, can easily require several orders of magnitude more computational time as well as more human oversight.
